topics.title: Health, Wellness, Illness & Social Determinants
topics.summary: Health is personal and keeps changing. Assess the whole person, including daily-life barriers, before you decide what wellness should look like.
objectives: You can tell health, wellness, disease, illness, and injury apart.
You can use the nine wellness dimensions to find strengths and concerns.
You can compare acute illness, chronic illness, remission, relapse, and exacerbation.
You can link the five social determinant areas to real nursing actions.
You can explain how illness changes family roles and caregiving.
You can spot when a chronic illness has a new, urgent change.
topics.bigPicture:
Two clients can have the same diagnosis and very different lives. One person with diabetes may feel capable, connected, and happy. Another person with no disease may feel tired, alone, and unsafe at home. A diagnosis matters, but it does not describe the whole person.

This lesson gives you a way to ask what matters to the client. It also helps you see what makes healthy choices possible, such as money, transport, and support. Nurses treat today’s problems, protect function, and help people reach their own goals. Wellness is still possible with chronic disease or disability.
recap: Health is a moving picture on a continuum, not a fixed label.
Disease is a body problem. Illness is how the person feels and lives it.
Wellness has nine dimensions and is possible during chronic illness.
Acute describes the course of an illness, not how severe it is.
Remission is not cure. A chronic illness can have an acute exacerbation.
A new change from baseline comes first, even in long-term disease.
Missed care is a cue to assess barriers, not proof the client does not care.
Willingness is not ability. Assess what the caregiver can safely do.

keyTerms.def: A changing experience of physical, mental, and social well-being. It is more than just having no disease.
An ongoing, self-directed process of making choices toward well-being.
How satisfied, purposeful, and emotionally well a person feels. A lab result cannot measure it.
A line from high wellness to serious illness. People move along it over time.
A change in body structure or function. It can be present even when the person feels fine.
The person’s own experience of feeling unwell. It can affect any wellness dimension.
Damage or loss of function caused by an event or exposure. It can be intentional or unintentional.
Illness that usually starts suddenly and lasts a short time. It can be mild or life-threatening.
Illness that lasts a long time and needs ongoing management. The course defines it as three months or longer.
Symptoms lessen or go away. It does not always mean the disease is cured.
Disease or symptoms come back after a period of improvement.
A flare, or worsening, of a condition the person already has.
Conditions where people live, learn, work, play, and worship that shape their health and chances.
A difference in health outcomes between groups. Look for the barriers and unfair conditions behind it.
The client explains or shows the teaching in their own words, so the nurse can check understanding.

sections.heading: What does being healthy mean?
sections.keyIdea: Health moves along a continuum over time, so ask each client what being healthy means to them.
sections.body:
The health-illness continuum is a line. One end is high wellness. The other end is serious illness. People move back and forth along it. It is not a label you assign at admission.

A person with a chronic condition can still sleep better, move more, or feel more connected. A person who feels well may have a silent disease that needs screening.

Ask, “What does being healthy mean to you?” and “What would you most like to be able to do?” Answers might be going back to work, going to worship, or caring for a grandchild. These goals connect your care plan to the client’s real life.

Do not assume the client shares your idea of wellness. Well-being includes meaning, satisfaction, and mood. A normal lab value cannot measure those things.
sections.analogy: A diagnosis is one photograph. The health-illness continuum is a movie. It shows symptoms, function, relationships, and resources changing over time.

sections.heading: What are the nine wellness dimensions?
sections.keyIdea: The nine dimensions affect each other, so a strength in one area can help a problem in another.
sections.body:
The course lists nine dimensions of wellness. They work together like gears. Stress in one area often spreads to others.

For example, money stress can lead to missed medicine, extra work shifts, poor sleep, and less time with friends. A good job can support identity. An unsafe workplace can harm the body.

Spiritual wellness is about meaning and purpose. It does not require religion. If a client says, “I’m not religious,” you can still ask what gives life meaning.

Look for strengths, not only problems. A reliable friend might drive the client to visits. Creative hobbies may help someone cope with a new disability.
bullets: Physical: activity, food, rest, and protective habits.
Emotional: noticing and expressing feelings.
Intellectual: learning and thinking.
Social: supportive relationships.
Spiritual: meaning and purpose, with or without religion.
Financial, career, creative, and environmental: money, work, self-expression, and a safe place to live.

rows: How are your energy, sleep, and mood?
Does work or cost make your care hard?
What do you enjoy learning or making?
Who supports you? What gives you meaning?
Do you have a safe place to live and be active?

sections.heading: Disease, illness, and injury: how do they differ?
sections.keyIdea: Disease is the body problem, illness is the person’s experience, and injury comes from an event or exposure.
sections.body:
Disease is a change in how the body is built or works. Illness is how the person feels and lives with a problem. The two do not always match.

A client with high blood pressure may have disease but feel fine. A client with months of fatigue may have illness before any test finds a disease. Do not dismiss symptoms because one test was normal.

Injury is damage or loss of function from an event or exposure. A fall can break a hip in a second. Years of loud noise can slowly damage hearing. So prevention covers both sudden hazards and repeated exposures.

Ask about work, home, activity, substances, and protective gear. Ask without blame. Your job is to find the risk and support safer conditions.

rows: Body structure or function has changed
BP 152/96 at three visits, but the client “feels fine”
Fatigue and joint aches with normal first labs
Damage from an event or repeated exposure
Hip fracture from a rug; hearing loss from leaf blowers

sections.heading: Acute or chronic: what is the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Acute and chronic describe how long an illness lasts, not how severe it is right now.
sections.body:
Acute illness usually starts suddenly and lasts a short time. It can be mild, like a cold, or life-threatening.

Chronic illness lasts a long time and needs ongoing care. Your course slides define chronic as three months or longer. Some diseases and tracking systems use other time rules.

A chronic illness can still flare. A client with asthma can have a sudden attack. That is an acute exacerbation on top of a chronic disease.

On the exam, do not assume “chronic” means stable. Do not assume “acute” means severe. Look at the current findings and the change from baseline.
bullets: Remission: symptoms ease or disappear. It is not always a cure, so follow-up still matters.
Relapse: the disease or symptoms come back after getting better.
Exacerbation: an existing condition gets worse.
sections.example: A client with COPD usually dresses alone. Today he stops for breath after every few words. His daughter says, “It’s just his lung disease.” This is a new change from baseline. Assess his breathing now.

sections.heading: What are social determinants of health?
sections.keyIdea: Social determinants decide whether a care plan is even possible, and teaching alone cannot fix a lack of food or transport.
sections.body:
Social determinants are the conditions of daily life that shape health. They include income, reading level, transport, housing, clean water, discrimination, and belonging.

A missed visit may mean no bus or no childcare. A client who skips the patient portal may have no internet or may find medical words confusing.

Ask concrete, neutral questions. “How do you get to appointments?” “Have you had trouble getting enough food?” “What gets in the way of taking this medicine?” Explain why you ask, and protect privacy.

Then match each barrier to a resource. Options include social work, low-cost pharmacy programs, interpreters, or a different appointment time.
bullets: Economic stability
Education access and quality
Health care access and quality
Neighborhood and built environment
Social and community context

rows: Coordinate safe storage and a workable plan
Use plain words, pictures, few key points, and teach-back
Find a safe activity option together
Says past clinics treated them badly
Listen and validate first, then advocate for respectful care
One neighborhood has more asthma ER visits
Assess conditions and access, not stereotypes about groups

sections.heading: How does illness affect the family?
sections.keyIdea: Illness changes roles at home, so assess both what the change means and what helpers can truly do.
sections.body:
Illness can change income, caregiving, intimacy, chores, and future plans. A person who cared for everyone may now need help bathing. A partner may take extra shifts. A teen may take over housework.

Ask the client who they consider family. Ask who they want involved. An alert client decides who receives their health information. The nearest relative is not automatically the decision partner.

Willingness does not prove ability. A spouse who says, “I’ll do everything,” may have back pain, work nights, or lack the skill. Watch them practice. Check their energy and health.

Support the client’s own role and independence. Doing everything for someone can increase feelings of uselessness. If a client feels role loss, explore which roles matter most to them.
bullets: Ask, “What has changed at home?”
Ask, “Who can help, and what can they actually do?”
Watch a return demonstration of any hands-on skill.
Offer practice, respite resources, equipment, or referral as needed.
If help at home cannot meet the client’s needs, escalate before discharge.

sections.heading: How do I turn assessment into a plan?
sections.keyIdea: Build the plan from the client’s priorities, barriers, and strengths, then check whether the barrier was actually removed.
sections.body:
Combine what the client tells you with what you observe. Subjective data are the client’s goals and symptoms. Objective data are things you see or measure, like gait or vital signs.

List problems, risks, and strengths together. A client can have poor mobility, a fall risk, and strong motivation all at once.

Write a goal that can be measured. For example: “By Friday, the client will name one affordable way to get the prescribed medicine.”

Then evaluate. Placing a referral is an action. The real outcome is the barrier being removed, such as the client getting to the next visit. If the plan fails, reassess. Never settle on “the client does not care.”
steps: Ask what matters most to the client.
Find the problems, risks, and strengths.
Match each barrier to a practical resource.
Set a measurable goal with the client.
Check the result and revise if needed.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers blame the client, trust a label, or skip a new change from baseline.
sections.body: These look-alike ideas cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Disease is the body change. Illness is the person’s experience. One can exist without the other.
Acute means sudden and short. It can be mild or deadly.
Chronic means long-lasting. It can still flare suddenly.
Remission means symptoms eased. Monitoring still finds relapse.
Missed care often comes from cost, transport, or literacy. Assess first.
A willing helper may lack strength, time, or skill. Verify.
New confusion is a change from baseline. Assess it right away.
A referral is an action. The outcome is the barrier removed.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the answer that assesses barriers or new changes first, respects the client, and fits real life.
sections.body:
Questions often give a label like “nonadherent” or “just his disease.” They test whether you look past it. Others ask you to sort clients by priority. A sudden change in a chronic illness usually wins over a stable resource need.

Here is a sample question. A client with diabetes missed two clinic visits. The client says, “I want to stay healthy, but I cannot keep doing this.” The chart says “nonadherent.” What should the nurse do first?
bullets: Common patterns: “what should the nurse do first,” “which finding needs follow-up,” and select-all barrier lists.
Priority questions mix an acute flare with stable wellness or access needs.
Hopeless statements, like “I don’t see the point,” need a direct question about suicide first.
steps: Read the stem: missed visits, a wish to stay healthy, and a label of nonadherence.
What is it really asking? Will you assess the reason or accept the label?
Key cues: “I want to stay healthy” is a strength. “I cannot keep doing this” hints at a barrier.
Wrong options: Reviewing complications assumes a knowledge gap. Having a caregiver schedule visits takes over before you know the problem. Phone reminders assume the client simply forgets.
The answer: Ask what is making it hard to get to visits, such as transport, cost, or work.
Strategy: When a client misses care, assess the barrier before you teach or judge.

sections.heading: Worked case: a plan that fails at home
sections.keyIdea: When a plan fails at home, find the real barriers and change the plan, not just the teaching.
sections.body:
Ms. R has stable diabetes. She wants to avoid another hospital stay. She can explain her medicines. Yet she has missed visits and buys cheap food that differs from her meal plan.

She cares for two grandchildren and rides the bus. These cues do not mean she lacks interest or knowledge. Her wish to stay well is a strength. Her clear explanation shows some understanding.

Transport, food cost, and caregiving are likely social determinants. Several barriers may be working together. Ask about each one. Keep checking her symptoms and safety, too.
steps: Name her strengths: she wants to stay well and knows her medicines.
Ask about each barrier: bus times, school pickup, and food money.
Match barriers to help: a new visit time, transport options, and affordable food resources.
Set a measurable goal, such as attending the next visit using the new plan.
Evaluate: did she get there, and can her household follow the plan?

check.q: Why is “teach the same plan again” not enough for Ms. R?
check.a: She already shows knowledge. Transport, cost, and caregiving may block action. More teaching cannot create money or time, so change the practical plan.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7 – Health, Wellness, Injury, Illness + Exemplars, slides 2–19 and 32–37.
The lesson paraphrases course concepts and uses original bedside examples.
The slides define chronic illness as lasting three months or longer. Other diseases and tracking systems may use other time rules.
Demographic statistics are not treated as fixed facts.

pearls: A diagnosis does not show how well a person functions or how they define wellness.
A chronic illness can flare. Prioritize the new change from baseline.
Assess resource barriers before blaming missed care on motivation.
Address health disparities by looking at access and conditions, not stereotypes.
Treat the urgent body problem first, then the social barrier that caused it.
An alert client chooses who counts as family and who gets information.
redFlags: New severe symptoms or fast loss of function need prompt assessment, even with a long-term diagnosis.
New confusion is never “just aging.” Compare with baseline and assess right away.
Hopeless statements, like “I don’t see the point anymore,” need a direct suicide-risk question.
Caregiver exhaustion, or no food, shelter, or medicine, can make a discharge plan unsafe.

checks.q: A client has had a blood pressure of 152/96 at three visits but says, “I feel fine, so I can’t have a disease.” How should the nurse respond?
checks.a: Explain that disease can be present without illness. High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so feeling well does not rule it out.

checks.q: A client misses visits because the bus route ended. What should the nurse assess?
checks.a: Transportation and access to care. Work with the client on a realistic option before assuming unwillingness.

checks.q: A client in remission from lymphoma plans to cancel all follow-up visits. What is the best response?
checks.a: Explain that remission is not the same as cure. Follow-up visits help find a relapse early.

checks.q: A home health client with Parkinson disease for 10 years has a new fall and new trouble swallowing. Is this “just the disease”?
checks.a: No. New changes from baseline in a chronic illness need prompt follow-up and assessment.

checks.q: An insulin user is skipping doses to save money and now has a glucose of 348 mg/dL with nausea. What comes first?
checks.a: Address the high glucose and symptoms first. Then work on the cost barrier with social work or pharmacy resources.

topics.title: Prevention, Health Beliefs & Behavior Change
topics.summary: Pick the prevention level by its purpose, match your approach to the client’s readiness, and build a plan the client can really carry out.
objectives: You can sort actions into primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
You can separate modifiable risk factors from ones that cannot change.
You can name a client’s stage of change from what they say.
You can respond to beliefs, locus of control, and low confidence.
You can write a measurable SMART-EST goal and revise it after a lapse.
You can respond safely when a client uses supplements or alternative care.
topics.bigPicture:
Health promotion helps people feel and function better. Prevention lowers the chance, severity, or harm of illness and injury. The two overlap. Teaching safe walking can build confidence and also prevent falls.

A perfect teaching sheet is useless if the goal does not matter to the client, the timing is wrong, or resources are missing. So the nurse starts by listening. Think of behavior change as a partnership. The client brings priorities and life experience. The nurse brings knowledge, support, and follow-up.
recap: Primary prevents a problem. Secondary finds it early. Tertiary limits harm from an existing problem.
Classify prevention by purpose and timing, not by whether the nurse is teaching.
Modifiable means changeable, not easy. Family history does not cancel lifestyle benefits.
Match your words to the stage of change. Explore beliefs before offering a plan.
Planning a change is preparation. Doing it is action.
A lapse is data. Explore the trigger and revise the plan together.
Good goals name an observable behavior, amount, time frame, and review date.
Ask about supplements without judgment, and coordinate review. Never stop therapy on your own.

keyTerms.def: Actions that help people increase well-being and function.
Action before a disease or injury happens, to stop it from occurring. Examples: vaccines, helmets.
Finding a condition early, often by screening people who have no known diagnosis.
Limiting harm and restoring function after a disease or injury already exists, such as rehab after a stroke.
A risk that can change, such as smoking, inactivity, or poor sleep.
A risk that cannot change, such as age or family history.
Whether a person believes their health depends mostly on their own actions (internal) or on fate, others, or luck (external).
A person’s belief that they can succeed at a specific action.
How willing and prepared a person is right now to change a behavior.
A short slip back into an old behavior during a change. It is not failure.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, evidence-based, strategic, and tailored.
A practice used along with conventional care, such as meditation.
A practice used instead of conventional care.
Care that combines suitable, evidence-informed approaches in one coordinated plan.

sections.heading: What are the three levels of prevention?
sections.keyIdea: Ask two questions: what condition is being targeted, and has it already happened?
sections.body:
Primary prevention acts before the problem starts. Vaccines and helmets are classic examples.

Secondary prevention finds a problem early, before symptoms. Screening is the key word. A blood pressure check for an adult with no known diagnosis is secondary.

Tertiary prevention limits harm from a problem that already exists. Rehab after a stroke is tertiary.

The same action can fit different levels. Exercise prevents disease in a healthy adult. It restores function in rehab. Teaching shows up at all three levels. So “the nurse teaches” does not automatically mean primary.

rows: Balance class for older adults who have never fallen
Vision screening for a teen with no known problem
Teaching monthly skin self-exams to an adult with no skin cancer
Energy conservation teaching for a client with COPD

sections.example: A student says a balance class for adults who never fell is secondary “because they are high risk.” Correct the student. No fall has happened yet, so the class is primary prevention.

sections.heading: How do community goals guide nursing?
sections.keyIdea: Population goals guide communities, but each client still needs an individual assessment.
sections.body:
The course names Healthy People 2030 and federal health programs. They set population goals, track progress, and draw attention to disparities.

A population goal is not a personal prescription. A national activity target does not tell you how far a client recovering from pneumonia should walk today. Start from that client’s assessed baseline.

Nurses work at several levels. With an individual, you might plan a safe walking routine. With a family, you might address smoke in the home. With a community, you might advocate for safe sidewalks or accessible clinics.

Measure outcomes, not just activity. Counting brochures handed out shows effort. Counting how many people got follow-up care, or learned a skill, shows real results.

sections.heading: How do risk factors and beliefs shape choices?
sections.keyIdea: Explore what the client believes before teaching, and build confidence with small wins.
sections.body:
Nonmodifiable risks include age and family history. Modifiable risks include tobacco, inactivity, poor sleep, and some eating patterns. Modifiable means changeable, not easy. Work hours, disability, food access, stress, and culture all shape choices.

Beliefs come from experience, family, culture, and past health care. Someone with an internal locus of control believes their actions matter. Someone with an external locus credits fate, God, other people, or luck. Neither label tells the full story, so ask.

Self-efficacy is confidence in doing one specific thing. Low confidence improves with small, achievable successes. More facts alone rarely help.
bullets: “My father had a heart attack, so it doesn’t matter what I do.” Explore the belief. Then explain that inherited and lifestyle risks both count.
“My health is in God’s hands.” Ask what that belief means for their care before building a plan.
“I never stick with anything.” Choose one tiny, doable step to build confidence.

sections.heading: What are the stages of change?
sections.keyIdea: Use the client’s own words to find their stage, then match your next step to that stage.
sections.body:
People move through stages when changing a habit. The path is not always a straight line. A slip, called a lapse, is a reason to find triggers and revise the plan. It does not prove change is impossible.

Do not hand a detailed quit plan to someone not yet thinking about quitting. And do not lecture about risks to someone who already has a plan. They need resources and follow-up.

The slides also list termination. That means the change is fully part of life. Not every behavior reaches it.

rows: “I don’t see a reason to stop.”
Explore beliefs. Offer information with permission.
“Part of me wants to, but I’m afraid.”
Explore the mixed feelings and confidence.
“I picked a quit date and downloaded an app.”
Help with concrete first steps and resources.
“I quit 3 weeks ago; evenings are hard.”
Troubleshoot triggers, affirm effort, arrange support.
Reinforce strategies and plan for setbacks.

sections.heading: How do I talk to build motivation?
sections.keyIdea: Open questions, reflection, and honest affirmation build motivation; blame, threats, and lectures shut it down.
sections.body:
Use open-ended questions to hear the client’s story. Reflect back what you heard, so the client can correct you. Affirm real effort, like “You found a way to eat vegetables even on double-shift days.”

Show empathy without saying you know exactly how they feel. Ask permission before giving information. Then use plain words and invite a response.

Let the client choose the first change. If a client smokes, sleeps five hours, and rarely exercises, ask which change feels most possible. Readiness predicts success better than the nurse’s ranking.

Remember: you can support an adult’s choices, but you cannot control them.

rows: “You want to cut back but drinking is how you unwind.”
“If you keep drinking, you’ll ruin your liver.”
“If you do this, you will never get sick.”

sections.heading: How do I write a SMART-EST goal?
sections.keyIdea: A strong goal names what the client will do, how much, how often, and when you will review it.
sections.body:
Use the nursing process, called ADPIE. Assess habits, beliefs, readiness, symptoms, resources, and support. Identify the problem, risk, or readiness to improve. Plan a shared goal. Implement the actions and referrals. Evaluate the results and revise.

SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. The course adds EST: evidence-based, strategic, and tailored.

“Exercise more” has no clear endpoint, so it cannot be measured. A better goal is: “For the next week, I will walk indoors for five minutes after breakfast on four days, as tolerated, and record symptoms.”

Fit the start point to the client. Do not give everyone the same amount. Set a review date.
steps: Ask the client to choose the behavior and say why it matters.
Assess ability, safety, readiness, and access.
Agree on an action, amount, frequency, and review date.
Plan support and a response to likely barriers.
Compare results with the goal and revise together.

sections.heading: What about supplements, support, and follow-up?
sections.keyIdea: Ask about every product without judgment, and coordinate review instead of stopping or adding therapy yourself.
sections.body:
Complementary therapy is used with regular care. Alternative therapy replaces it. Integrative care blends suitable, evidence-informed approaches into one plan.

Ask about supplements, traditional practices, and relaxation methods. Record the details. “Natural” does not mean safe. A client on warfarin who starts ginkgo needs a pharmacist or prescriber review.

Replacing a prescribed drug is a bigger safety concern. If a client stopped a blood pressure pill for an herbal product, first check the current blood pressure and the product. Then coordinate with the provider.

At follow-up, ask what actually happened. If a client met a goal on only two of eight days, affirm progress and find the barrier. Then revise the plan together.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most traps confuse the action with its purpose, or the nurse’s timeline with the client’s readiness.
sections.body: Use this table to separate ideas that look alike on exam questions.

rows: Teaching can be any level. Ask if the condition already exists.
High risk with no problem yet is still primary.
Screening finds a problem early. That is secondary.
Planning steps is preparation. Doing the behavior is action.
A lapse is a slip. Explore triggers and revise.
Complementary adds to care. Alternative replaces it, which raises safety concerns.
Targets guide populations. Start each client at their baseline.
Brochures handed out is activity. People getting care is outcome.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Identify the stage or prevention level from the stem, then choose the response that fits it.
sections.body:
Expect “which level of prevention” items, select-all lists, and stage-of-change statements. You may also see goal-writing items and follow-up after a lapse.

Sample question: A client says, “My grandfather smoked until he was 90. I don’t see any reason to quit.” Which response is best?
steps: Read the stem: the client sees no reason to change.
What is it really asking? Which stage is this, and what fits that stage?
Key cues: “I don’t see any reason” shows precontemplation.
Wrong options: Choosing a quit date skips ahead to preparation. Warning about lung disease is a threat. Saying the grandfather was lucky argues with the client.
The answer: An open question, such as “What do you enjoy about smoking, and has anything about it ever worried you?” It explores beliefs first.
Strategy: Name the stage from the client’s words, then pick the matching action.

sections.heading: Worked case: readiness changes the next step
sections.keyIdea: Mixed feelings mean contemplation, so explore them before you offer a quit plan.
sections.body:
Mr. J says he is thinking about quitting tobacco. He worries it is his only way to cope with stressful shifts. He has not set a date.

A detailed quit calendar now gives good information at the wrong time. He is in contemplation. Explore what he likes and dislikes about smoking and what else helps with stress.

Reflect without approving the risk: “You want the health benefit, but you worry about losing a way to cope.” Later, if he picks a date and gathers help, he is in preparation. If he lapses after starting, explore the trigger. Do not treat the lapse as proof he was not serious.
steps: Use his words to find his stage: contemplation.
Explore mixed feelings before assuming commitment.
Ask what support he would find useful.
Build concrete steps once he is preparing.
After a lapse, review triggers and revise the plan.

check.q: What would show Mr. J moving from contemplation to preparation?
check.a: A specific plan with practical steps, such as choosing a quit date and arranging support. Knowing the risks alone is not preparation.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, slides 20–37 and 49.
Prevention levels, stages of change, locus of control, integrative care, and SMART-EST come from the course slides.
Examples are original applications of those concepts.

mnemonics.name: Prevent, Screen, Support
mnemonics.text: Primary = Prevent it. Secondary = Screen for it. Tertiary = Support recovery and limit harm.

pearls: Education can be primary, secondary, or tertiary. Classify by purpose.
Screening people with no known diagnosis is secondary prevention.
Use the client’s stated readiness, not your enthusiasm, to choose the next step.
A measurable behavior beats “understands healthy living.”
Low confidence improves with small successes, not more information.
Evaluate programs by whether people got care or changed behavior.
redFlags: New exertional symptoms, like chest pain with activity, need evaluation before any exercise plan.
A client who replaced a prescribed drug with an unreviewed product needs assessment and coordination now.
Supplements can interact with drugs like warfarin. Coordinate pharmacist or prescriber review.

checks.q: A client with COPD learns energy conservation. Which level of prevention is this?
checks.a: Tertiary. The disease already exists, and the goal is to reduce its impact and support function.

checks.q: A client has chosen a quit date but has not stopped smoking. Which stage fits?
checks.a: Preparation. Planning and gathering resources come before action.

checks.q: What is wrong with the goal “the client will understand exercise”?
checks.a: It cannot be observed. State what the client will do or show, how much, and when you will check.

checks.q: A client who quit smoking two months ago smoked three cigarettes at a party. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Explore the trigger, recognize the progress made, and revise the plan together. Do not call it failure.

checks.q: A nursing student says a client recovering from pneumonia “needs 150 minutes of activity this week.” What is the problem?
checks.a: That is a population target. Start from the client’s assessed baseline and progress gradually.

topics.title: Physical Fitness, Exercise & Safe Activity
topics.summary: Learn the types and benefits of exercise, then fit activity to the client’s ability, goals, symptoms, and surroundings, and know when to stop.
objectives: You can tell physical activity, exercise, and fitness apart.
You can match aerobic, strength, flexibility, and balance work to a goal.
You can name isotonic, isometric, and isokinetic exercise from what the joint does.
You can use the talk test and lifespan guidelines safely.
You can name the stop-and-report symptoms during activity.
You can plan, delegate, and evaluate activity care.
topics.bigPicture:
Physical activity is any movement that uses muscles and energy. Exercise is planned, repeated activity done to improve fitness. Walking to the bus is activity. A planned walking routine to build stamina is exercise.

Nursing care starts with what the client can safely do today. The goal is better function and real participation in life. People who use wheelchairs, have chronic disease, or are deconditioned can still exercise. Their plan is simply adapted. Progress is measured against their own starting point, with close attention to symptoms.
recap: Activity is any energy-using movement. Exercise is planned activity to build fitness.
Isometric: muscle tightens, joint does not move. Isotonic: the joint moves.
Isokinetic means machine-controlled constant speed, not just “using a machine.”
Talk test: moderate means you can talk but not sing. Vigorous means only a few words.
Adults: 150–300 moderate or 75–150 vigorous minutes weekly, plus strength work on 2 or more days.
Children and teens: at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.
Stop and assess for chest discomfort, severe new breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting.
Guidelines are targets, not starting doses. Start from the client’s baseline.

keyTerms.def: Any body movement that uses skeletal muscles and energy.
Planned, repeated physical activity done to improve or maintain fitness.
The capacity and well-being supported by activity, nutrition, sleep, and other healthy habits.
Steady activity that relies mostly on oxygen to make energy, like brisk walking or cycling.
Short, very hard effort that relies mostly on energy pathways not needing oxygen, like a sprint.
The muscle changes length and the joint moves against resistance, like a biceps curl.
The muscle tightens but the joint does not move, like a quadriceps set.
Movement at a constant, machine-controlled speed, usually with special rehab equipment.
Holding the breath while straining. It can spike blood pressure during isometric effort.
A simple way to judge exercise intensity by how easily a person can talk.
The ability to finish an activity with a safe body response and manageable symptoms.
Loss of strength and stamina from illness or inactivity.
Feeling about to faint, often with dizziness or vision changes.

sections.heading: Why does activity matter to clients?
sections.keyIdea: Activity helps body and mind, but tie it to a goal the client values instead of promising cures.
sections.body:
Regular activity builds endurance, strength, balance, coordination, and mobility. It helps control blood pressure and blood sugar. It supports bone strength and independence.

Activity also helps the mind. It can improve mood, lower stress, improve sleep, and create social connection.

Do not promise too much. Exercise does not prevent every disease or cure a chronic condition. For a client with depression, say exercise can help mood, but it does not replace treatment.

Ask which benefit matters most. A client may care more about gardening again than about lowering a future risk. A functional goal makes the plan real and motivating.
sections.example: An older adult wants to attend a community meal. The plan may combine walking endurance, safe transfers, balance work, and transport help. It does not need to focus only on weight.

sections.heading: What types of exercise are there?
sections.keyIdea: Pick the exercise type that matches the client’s goal and ability, not the hardest option available.
sections.body:
Aerobic activity includes brisk walking, swimming, dancing, and cycling. Anaerobic efforts are short and intense, like sprints or heavy lifting. Most activities use both energy systems. The terms describe the main demand, not whether the body has oxygen.

Interval training switches between hard and easy effort. It is not automatically right for a beginner or someone medically unstable.

A full plan often mixes several types. Match the activity to the goal and to what the client can do now.

rows: Use good technique and a safe load. Supports muscles and bones.
Assess fall risk and need for supervision.

sections.heading: Isotonic, isometric, or isokinetic?
sections.keyIdea: Name the type by what the joint does: moves, stays still, or moves at a machine-controlled speed.
sections.body:
Isotonic exercise moves a joint against resistance. The muscle changes length. Examples are biceps curls, rising from a chair, and climbing stairs.

Isometric exercise tightens a muscle while the joint stays still. Examples are a quadriceps set and a wall sit. It keeps muscles strong when a joint cannot move, such as in a cast or after surgery that limits motion.

Isometric effort can raise blood pressure sharply, especially if the client holds their breath. Teach clients to keep breathing. Use caution with heart disease, as the care plan directs.

Isokinetic exercise uses special equipment that keeps the speed constant. A treadmill or a regular stationary bike is not isokinetic just because it is a machine.
sections.analogy: Isotonic: lift and lower a grocery bag. Isometric: push against a wall that will not move. Isokinetic: a rehab machine sets the speed for you.
sections.example: A client in a long leg cast wants to keep thigh strength. Teach quadriceps sets, which are isometric. Remind the client to breathe normally during each hold.

sections.heading: How hard is the client working?
sections.keyIdea: Moderate means the client can talk but not sing; vigorous means only a few words before a breath.
sections.body:
The talk test is a quick way to judge intensity. It works for stable clients. It does not replace assessment or rehab orders.

Some drugs change the body’s response. Beta blockers, such as metoprolol, keep the heart rate low. A client on one may never reach a heart rate target on a watch. Guide intensity by the talk test and symptoms instead.

The talk test shows intensity. It does not show the total amount of activity for the week.

rows: Can talk but cannot sing comfortably
Can say only a few words before pausing for breath

bullets: Teach a warm-up first.
Use safe footwear and proper equipment.
Progress slowly from the starting point.
Keep breathing normally. Do not hold the breath.
Know which symptoms mean stop and who to call.

sections.heading: How much activity is recommended?
sections.keyIdea: Guidelines are weekly or daily targets for populations, so start each client where they are and build up.
sections.body:
School-age children and teens need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day. This includes muscle- and bone-strengthening activity. Gym class twice a week is not enough.

Adults aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity. They also need muscle strengthening on at least two days. These are weekly totals. An adult who walks 25 minutes six days a week meets the aerobic goal but still needs strength work.

Older adults follow the adult targets as able and add balance and functional activity. People with chronic conditions or disability should be as active as their abilities allow. The slides describe 150 moderate minutes a week for an uncomplicated pregnancy, coordinated with the obstetric team.

rows: Start with short, doable bouts. Build up slowly.
Add balance and functional strength with safety support.
Adapt activity and equipment to function and the care plan.
Consider complications and prior activity. Coordinate with the obstetric team.

sections.example: A sedentary adult says, “I need 150 minutes, so I’ll walk 150 minutes on Saturday.” Explain that 150 is a weekly total. Start with shorter walks and build up.

sections.heading: What should I assess before recommending activity?
sections.keyIdea: Check safety, ability, confidence, and access before you suggest any activity plan.
sections.body:
Ask about usual activity, symptoms, falls, pain, devices, injuries, and what the client enjoys. Review diagnoses, restrictions, and medicines.

Ability and confidence differ. A client may be strong enough to walk but afraid of falling again. Another may be willing but have no safe place to walk. “Join a gym” fails if the client cannot afford it.

Assess readiness, too. A client in contemplation may need to talk about fears first. A client who is preparing may need help picking a safe start.

Refer to physical or occupational therapy for rehab and equipment needs.
steps: Assess baseline ability, symptoms, restrictions, and fall risk.
Ask about fears, preferences, cost, and a safe place to be active.
Write a SMART goal with the client: activity, amount, frequency, and review date.
Teach technique and have the client show it back.
Evaluate distance, assistance, symptoms, recovery time, and function.

sections.heading: When must activity stop?
sections.keyIdea: New chest discomfort, severe breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting means stop now and assess.
sections.body:
Pain is not proof that exercise is working. Sharp pain during exercise means stop and assess.

If a client feels faint while walking, stop and get them safely seated first. Then assess.

Review unstable illness with the provider before starting or advancing exercise. A client with very high blood pressure should not start a high-intensity class tomorrow. In pregnancy, a warning sign means stop and get prompt obstetric evaluation.

The RN can delegate routine walks for stable clients to assistive personnel (UAP). The RN keeps assessment, teaching, evaluation, and decisions to progress. If a UAP reports chest symptoms after a walk, the RN assesses the client personally and promptly.
bullets: New chest discomfort or pressure
Severe or new shortness of breath
Dizziness or near-fainting
Sharp new pain

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Classify by mechanism and judge readiness by assessment, not by motivation or minutes.
sections.body: These pairs look alike on the exam. Here is how to tell them apart.

rows: Joint still is isometric. Joint moving is isotonic.
Isokinetic requires controlled constant speed. A self-paced bike is not.
Talk but not sing is moderate. Few words only is vigorous.
150 minutes is per week, not all at once or per day.
Adults also need strength work on 2 or more days.
Eagerness is not a safety check. Assess tolerance first.
Expected soreness differs from chest pain or near-fainting.
Track endurance, recovery, function, and confidence.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Safety symptoms beat targets, and the RN keeps assessment, teaching, and evaluation.
sections.body:
Expect contraction-type items, talk-test items, and guideline numbers. Priority items ask which client in a walking program needs follow-up first. Delegation items ask which activity task fits a UAP.

Sample question: A stable client begins a planned walk and reports new chest pressure and marked shortness of breath. What should the nurse do first?
steps: Read the stem: a stable client, a planned walk, new chest pressure, and marked breathlessness.
What is it really asking? Does a red-flag symptom override the exercise plan?
Key cues: “New” and “marked” signal a change, not normal effort.
Wrong options: Lowering the intensity keeps the client exercising. Checking the pulse against a training range puts a number ahead of symptoms. Walking back to document first delays assessment.
The answer: Stop the activity, help the client rest safely, and assess right away.
Strategy: If a symptom suggests heart or breathing trouble, stop first and assess.

sections.heading: Worked case: function before a target
sections.keyIdea: A valued goal guides the plan, but assess tolerance and route safety before starting.
sections.body:
Mrs. B fell two months ago. She uses a cane indoors and tires quickly. She wants to walk to a nearby shop again. The route has uneven pavement.

A weekly activity target is background only. It does not prove she can do this route safely today. Ask what the shop visit means to her. It might be independence, friendship, or getting food.

A therapist can check her technique and device. Community services can help with access while she builds endurance. Teach her the stop signs. Moderate effort is expected. New chest pressure means stop and get help.
steps: Connect activity to her goal: walking to the shop.
Assess baseline walking, symptoms, falls, device, and the route.
Pick a safe start, such as short indoor walks with rests.
Teach stop-and-report symptoms.
Evaluate with details, like “walked 5 minutes with one rest, no symptoms.”

check.q: Why does meeting a weekly minute target not prove Mrs. B is ready for the shop route?
check.a: The route also needs balance on uneven ground, safe device use, and enough reserve for the trip. Minutes alone do not show those abilities.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.A, slides 38–49.
Isokinetic exercise is defined by constant, controlled speed. The slide lists broad equipment examples, but ordinary exercise machines do not meet this definition by themselves.
Activity targets still require individual assessment.

mnemonics.name: Three “iso” words
mnemonics.text: Isometric = muscle tight, joint motionless. Isotonic = joint moves (think “toning” with curls). Isokinetic = kept at constant speed by a machine.

pearls: Classify exercise by joint movement and mechanism, not by equipment name.
Moderate intensity: the client can talk but not sing.
With a beta blocker, guide intensity by the talk test and symptoms.
Individualize guideline totals to current capacity.
Document distance, assistance, symptoms, and recovery, not “tolerated well.”
Delegate routine walks for stable clients. Keep assessment, teaching, and evaluation.
redFlags: Stop activity and assess for new chest discomfort, severe breathlessness, dizziness, or near-fainting.
If a client feels faint while walking, get them safely seated first, then assess.
Review unstable illness, new injury, or restrictions before starting or advancing activity.
A warning sign during pregnancy means stop and get prompt obstetric evaluation.

checks.q: A client tightens the thigh muscle while the knee stays still. What type of contraction is this?
checks.a: Isometric. The muscle develops tension without joint movement.

checks.q: A student says a client riding a stationary bike at a self-chosen pace is doing isokinetic exercise. Is that right?
checks.a: No. Isokinetic exercise needs controlled constant speed, usually with special equipment.

checks.q: A runner can say only a few words before taking a breath. What intensity is this, and how many minutes a week meet the aerobic minimum?
checks.a: Vigorous. Seventy-five vigorous minutes a week meets the adult aerobic minimum.

checks.q: A parent says her 9-year-old has gym twice a week, so she gets enough exercise. How should the nurse respond?
checks.a: Explain that school-age children need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.

checks.q: What should the nurse assess before recommending daily outdoor walking?
checks.a: Baseline ability, symptoms, fall risk, devices, restrictions, preferences, and a safe, accessible route.

topics.title: Oral Health, Assessment & Daily Care
topics.summary: Oral care supports comfort, eating, speech, and dignity. Assess the mouth, the client’s ability to do care, swallowing safety, and access to dental services.
objectives: You can describe the main mouth structures and what saliva does.
You can tell plaque, tartar, cavities, gingivitis, and periodontal disease apart.
You can assess oral habits, function, risk, and access to dental care.
You can teach current fluoride and first dental visit guidance for children.
You can give safe oral care to clients with aspiration risk or dentures.
You can decide what to delegate and how to evaluate oral care.
topics.bigPicture:
A sore or dry mouth makes it hard to eat, talk, swallow, and socialize. A client who cannot grip a toothbrush, or cannot remember the steps, may lose oral health even after teaching. Oral care is a nursing assessment and comfort issue. It is not just about looks.

Look beyond the teeth. Check lips, gums, tongue, the inside lining of the mouth, saliva, dentures, pain, and how much the client can do. Nurses keep the mouth clean and comfortable. They also arrange dental care for disease, lasting sores, or tooth pain.
recap: Oral health supports eating, speaking, comfort, and dignity.
Plaque is a soft film. Tartar is hardened plaque that needs professional removal.
Brushing can help early enamel changes. It cannot fix an established cavity.
Bleeding gums need gentle, continued brushing and assessment, never stopping care.
Under age 3: a rice-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth.
Dental home by the first tooth, and no later than the first birthday.
Aspiration risk changes how oral care is done, not whether it is done.
Facial swelling with fever, drooling, or trouble swallowing is an airway emergency.

keyTerms.def: Chewing. It is the mechanical start of digestion.
The moist pink lining inside the mouth and cheeks.
The hard outer covering of the visible tooth crown.
The soft inner part of a tooth that holds nerves and blood vessels.
An enzyme in saliva that starts breaking down starches.
A soft, sticky film of bacteria on the teeth.
Hardened plaque. Routine brushing cannot remove it; a dental professional must.
Tooth decay. Bacteria turn sugars and starches into acid that damages the tooth.
Gum inflammation, often with redness, swelling, and bleeding.
Disease of the deeper tissues that hold teeth in place. It can cause gum recession and loose teeth.
An older term in the source for advanced gum disease with pus.
Dry mouth, often from less saliva due to medicines or illness.
An ongoing relationship with one dental office for regular care.
Fluid, food, or secretions entering the airway and lungs.
Difficulty swallowing.
Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as nursing assistants. The RN delegates routine tasks for stable clients to them.

sections.heading: Why does the mouth matter?
sections.keyIdea: The mouth starts digestion and supports speech, so dryness or pain can quietly reduce eating.
sections.body:
The mouth includes lips, cheeks, teeth, gums, tongue, palate, and salivary glands. The visible crown of a tooth is covered in enamel. Inside is the pulp, with nerves and blood vessels. The root anchors the tooth.

Teeth break up food. The tongue moves food and helps with taste and speech. Saliva moistens food, helps swallowing, and rinses the mouth. Its enzyme, amylase, starts breaking down starch.

A dry mouth makes talking and chewing uncomfortable. It also raises the risk of decay. Do not assume dryness is just part of aging. Review fluids, medicines, illness, and ability to do care.

A client may skip meals because chewing hurts. Address the mouth, not just the intake numbers.

sections.heading: Plaque, tartar, cavities, or gum disease?
sections.keyIdea: Soft plaque responds to daily care, while hard tartar and real cavities need a dentist.
sections.body:
Plaque bacteria feed on sugars and starches. They make acid that damages teeth. Risks for decay include frequent sugar, too little brushing, low fluoride, and dry mouth.

Early enamel changes, before a hole forms, may repair with fluoride and good care. This is called remineralization. An established cavity does not heal with brushing. It needs dental repair.

Plaque can harden into tartar, which needs professional cleaning. Gingivitis makes gums red, swollen, and bleeding. Periodontal disease goes deeper. It can cause receding gums and loose teeth.

Bleeding gums are a cue to assess technique and tissue and to refer. They are not a reason to stop brushing.

rows: Arrange dental cleaning. Keep up daily care.
Gentle brushing, assess, and refer as needed.
Receding gums, loose teeth, or pus
Find the cause and offer safe moisture.

sections.heading: What should the oral assessment include?
sections.keyIdea: Assess habits, mouth findings, the client’s ability to do care, and access to a dentist.
sections.body:
Inspect with good light and proper precautions. Record exact sites and findings, not “mouth bad.” Compare with earlier findings.

Check function. Can the client open containers, grip a brush, see the supplies, follow steps, and handle secretions? Weak hands, memory loss, fatigue, and pain each need a different fix.

Some clients need extra assessment and special plans. These include clients with diabetes, weak immune systems, poor nutrition, oral surgery, or head and neck radiation. Age alone is not a reason.

Medicines can cause dry mouth or gum changes. Report concerns to the prescriber. Never stop a prescribed drug on your own.
bullets: Brushing, products, and flossing habits
Last dental visit, plus cost and transport barriers
Pain, bleeding, swelling, sores, or taste changes
Tobacco use, diet, and swallowing
New medicines, such as an antidepressant causing dry mouth
sections.example: A resident with advanced dementia cannot describe pain. She has refused meals for 3 days and guards her jaw. Inspect her mouth first. Pain there may be the cause.

sections.heading: How do I protect children’s teeth?
sections.keyIdea: Start fluoride brushing at the first tooth and set up a dental home by the first birthday.
sections.body:
Do not put a child to bed with a bottle of milk, formula, or sweet drinks. Long, repeated exposure feeds decay.

Baby teeth matter. They support chewing, speech, and spacing for adult teeth. They are not throwaway practice teeth.

Caregivers brush or supervise based on the child’s skill. The slide suggests water-only brushing at 18 months and a first dental visit by six months. Current guidance differs, as shown below.

Chalky white bands or brown spots near the gumline of a toddler’s front teeth suggest decay. The child needs a dental evaluation and a dental home. Remove sugary bedtime bottles.
bullets: Under age 3: brush twice daily with a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste, about the size of a grain of rice.
Ages 3 to 6: use a pea-sized amount, with supervision.
Set up a dental home when the first tooth appears, and no later than the first birthday.
Higher risk or symptoms may need an earlier visit.
sections.example: A parent of an 18-month-old asks how to brush. Teach caregiver brushing with a rice-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste. Ask whether the child has a dentist yet.

sections.heading: What changes in pregnancy and older age?
sections.keyIdea: Pregnancy and aging bring new risks, but neither one is a reason to skip dental care.
sections.body:
Pregnancy can make gums more inflamed and likely to bleed. Vomiting or reflux bathes teeth in acid. Encourage gentle brushing and a dental visit. Pregnancy is not a reason to avoid routine dental care.

Older adults may have dry mouth, chronic disease, medicine effects, dentures, stiff hands, or memory loss. Age alone does not mean dependence or tooth loss.

Preserve independence. Use thick-handled or electric brushes, reminders, or set-up help. For a client with dementia who pushes the brush away, try simple cues, a set routine, and letting her do what she can.

Moisture can include saliva substitutes and sips of water if swallowing is safe and fluids are allowed. With a fluid restriction, use oral care and moisture products that stay within the fluid plan.
bullets: Dentures: clean them, store them in a labeled cup, and inspect the gums underneath.
A red, sore spot under a denture needs inspection and a fit check. Do not just add adhesive.
Involve the alert client in their own denture care.

sections.heading: How do I give oral care safely?
sections.keyIdea: For a client who cannot protect the airway, position side-lying, use little fluid, and suction as needed.
sections.body:
Explain the care, offer privacy, and let the client help as able. Use a soft brush. Fragile tissue may need extra-gentle cleaning.

Clients with low alertness, swallowing problems, or poor secretion control are at risk of aspiration. Protecting the airway comes first.

Position them as their condition allows, often side-lying with the head turned. This lets fluid drain out of the mouth, not into the airway. Use suction when needed. Never pour fluid into the mouth.

Clients who are NPO or on tube feedings still need oral care. NPO means nothing by mouth. Follow the care plan for how often. The slide’s range of every two to eight hours does not replace a risk assessment.
steps: Assess alertness, swallowing, mouth findings, pain, and cooperation.
Explain the care and position the client safely.
Clean gently while controlling fluid and secretions with suction.
Inspect dentures and tissues, and add safe moisture.
Record findings, help given, tolerance, and follow-up.
sections.example: Right after oral care, a client with low alertness starts gurgling and the oxygen level drops. Clear the airway first. Call for help and document after.

sections.heading: Who does oral care, and did it work?
sections.keyIdea: Delegate routine care for stable clients, keep risky care yourself, and judge success by the client’s change.
sections.body:
The RN can delegate routine oral care for stable clients to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). The RN keeps care that needs assessment. That includes a new or unknown swallowing risk, airway risk, or a new finding.

If a UAP says, “His gums bled, so I stopped brushing,” teach that bleeding gums need gentle brushing and assessment, not no brushing. If a delegated task creates an immediate choking risk, stop it and protect the airway first.

Evaluate outcomes. Giving an adapted brush is an intervention. The outcome is the client using it, with less pain and healthier tissue. For a caregiver, watch a safe return demonstration.
bullets: Ask about comfort. Look for less debris and dryness.
Can the client eat or speak more easily?
Persistent sores, tooth pain, swelling, pus, unexplained bleeding, or loose teeth need evaluation.
Oral and body disease are linked, but do not claim one always causes the other.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Do not let a label, an old belief, or a delivered intervention replace assessment.
sections.body: These look-alike ideas often appear in wrong answer choices.

rows: Plaque is soft and brushes off. Tartar is hard and needs a dentist.
Early changes can remineralize. A cavity needs restoration.
Red, bleeding gums are gingivitis. Recession and loose teeth are deeper disease.
Dryness has causes. Assess medicines, fluids, and illness.
NPO changes how care is done, not whether it is needed.
Keep brushing gently. Assess and refer.
A painful mouth can be the real reason for eating less.
Outcome means the client uses it with better comfort.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Airway safety comes first, then comfort and function, then teaching and referral.
sections.body:
Expect priority items about drowsy or unresponsive clients, select-all lists of urgent findings, and pediatric fluoride questions. Delegation items ask which client’s oral care fits a UAP.

Sample question: A drowsy client with poor secretion control needs oral care. Which action is the priority before cleaning begins?
steps: Read the stem: drowsy client, poor secretion control, oral care.
What is it really asking? What protects this client from aspiration?
Key cues: “Drowsy” and “poor secretion control” mean airway risk.

Wrong options: Choosing a product and cleaning first skips the airway. Cleaning dentures before checking rinse safety is out of order. Asking about home routines while setting up a standard rinse ignores the risk.
The answer: Assess airway safety and prepare side-lying positioning and suction.
Strategy: When swallowing or alertness is impaired, protect the airway before anything else.

sections.heading: Worked case: poor intake starts in the mouth
sections.keyIdea: When intake drops and the mouth hurts, treat the mouth problem as a possible cause.
sections.body:
An older adult eats little and says food tastes bad. Her mouth is dry. Her dentures hurt. Stiff hands make brushing hard.

Calling this a nutrition knowledge problem and handing over a food sheet misses the cause. Her appetite may be fine. Mouth pain may stop her from eating.

Check swallowing safety before offering water sips. If fluids are restricted, keep moisture care within the plan. Do not stop a medicine just because it may cause dryness. Report it instead.
steps: Assess mouth pain, denture fit, tissue, saliva, swallowing, medicines, and fluid limits.
Ask which problem started first and what happens when she eats.
Give gentle help, safe moisture, and an adapted brush.
Arrange a dental visit she can actually get to.
Reassess chewing, comfort, intake, and whether she can use the brush.

check.q: In this case, what is an intervention and what is an outcome?
check.a: Giving an adapted brush is an intervention. The client using it well, with better comfort and eating, is the outcome.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.B, slides 50–58.
Update: the slide suggests water-only brushing at 18 months and a first dental visit by six months.
Current AAPD parent guidance and periodicity schedule: tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste under age 3; pea-sized amount ages 3 to 6.
Current AAPD guidance: dental home at the first tooth and no later than the first birthday. Checked October 27, 2026.
This is a stated clinical update, not a quote from the slide.
The slide’s two-to-eight-hour special-care range does not replace individual risk assessment.

pearls: Assess dry mouth for a cause instead of calling it normal aging.
Trouble swallowing changes the oral-care technique, not the need for it.
Prevention starts with the first tooth.
Brushing does not reverse an established cavity.
For a hands-on caregiver skill, evaluate with a return demonstration.
Diabetes, weak immunity, oral surgery, and head and neck radiation call for special oral plans.
redFlags: Facial swelling with fever, drooling, voice change, or trouble swallowing or breathing needs urgent action.
Low alertness and poor secretion control raise aspiration risk during oral care.
Gurgling or a drop in oxygen after oral care means clear the airway first.
Lasting sores, loose teeth, or pus need dental evaluation.

checks.q: How do plaque and tartar differ?
checks.a: Plaque is a soft bacterial film that brushing removes. Tartar is hardened plaque that needs professional removal.

checks.q: What changes when a drowsy client needs oral care?
checks.a: Protect the airway: side-lying position with the head turned, very little fluid, and suction as needed.

checks.q: How much fluoride toothpaste is used for a child under age 3?
checks.a: A tiny smear, about the size of a grain of rice, brushed by the caregiver from the first tooth.

checks.q: A client with heart failure on a 1,500 mL fluid restriction has a very dry mouth. What helps?
checks.a: Frequent oral care and moisture support that stays within the fluid limit, such as saliva substitutes.

checks.q: An older adult cannot grip a toothbrush. Is more explanation enough?
checks.a: No. Assess function, provide an adapted brush or help, and check that the client can actually do the care.

topics.title: Normal Sleep, Circadian Rhythm & Nursing Care
topics.summary: Assess both how much and how well a client sleeps, know normal age changes, and target the real causes of poor rest safely.
objectives: You can explain how sleep supports thinking, healing, and mood.
You can describe circadian rhythm and the N1, N2, N3, and REM stages.
You can tell normal age-related sleep changes from warning signs.
You can assess sleep onset, waking, quality, and daytime function.
You can choose sleep interventions that keep required care safe.
You can recognize when sleepiness is a danger sign.
topics.bigPicture:
Sleep is an active body process, not just “switching off.” The brain cycles through stages while awareness of the room fades. Sleep restores the body, builds memory, steadies emotions, and supports daily function.

Pain, stress, medicines, illness, and hospital routines can all break up sleep. So ask two questions: “How much are you sleeping?” and “How rested do you feel during the day?” Eight hours in bed may include many awakenings. Your nursing response depends on the pattern, its causes, and what the client wants.
recap: Hours in bed do not equal hours asleep. Assess quality and daytime function.
Current staging has three NREM stages (N1, N2, N3) plus REM.
Deep N3 sleep comes mostly early in the night. REM gets longer toward morning.
Older adults sleep lighter and earlier, but they do not need much less sleep.
Find and treat the cause, like pain, noise, or nocturia, before asking for a sleeping pill.
Cluster nonurgent care, but never skip required monitoring to protect sleep.
A client who cannot be awakened is not “just sleeping.” Assess immediately.
Alcohol may help a person fall asleep but disrupts sleep later.

keyTerms.def: The body’s roughly 24-hour clock. It times sleepiness, alertness, temperature, and hormones.
A hormone that rises in darkness and signals that it is night.
A brainstem network involved in staying awake and alert.
Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep. It now has three stages: N1, N2, and N3.
Deep, slow-wave sleep. It is the most restorative stage and decreases with age.
Rapid-eye-movement sleep. The brain is active, dreams are common, and muscles normally relax.
The time a person actually spends asleep.
How restful and satisfying sleep feels, including how often it is broken and how the person feels the next day.
Habits and surroundings that support regular, restful sleep.
A daily log of sleep times, awakenings, naps, substances, symptoms, and daytime function.
Waking at night to urinate.
Sleep broken up by many awakenings.
A medicine that causes drowsiness or sleep. It can slow breathing and cause confusion or falls.
Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as nursing assistants. They can do routine tasks but not assessment.

sections.heading: Why does sleep matter so much?
sections.keyIdea: Lost sleep harms attention, memory, mood, healing, and safety, so a rest plan is part of recovery.
sections.body:
Too little sleep, or broken sleep, can weaken attention, memory, reaction time, judgment, and emotional control. That affects walking safely, managing medicines, learning, and driving.

Sleep also supports tissue repair and immune function. So the rest plan belongs next to the pain, mobility, and recovery plans.

Ask about daytime function, not just trouble sleeping. A quiet client may be too exhausted to learn. A caregiver who is up all night with a loved one may report mood changes and trouble with daily tasks.

Poor sleep can be a problem by itself. It can also be a clue to another problem, like pain, breathing trouble, or a medicine effect.
sections.example: A client keeps dozing during insulin teaching after a night of pain. Treat the pain, reschedule key teaching, and check learning later. Do not chart “uninterested.”

sections.heading: How does the body clock work?
sections.keyIdea: Light and darkness set the body clock, so bright days and dark nights help reset it.
sections.body:
The circadian rhythm is the body’s 24-hour clock. Light and darkness are its main cues. Melatonin usually rises in the dark and tells the body it is night.

Shift work, irregular schedules, bright rooms at night, and frequent interruptions can throw the clock off. A hospital client who naps all day and is wide awake at night may have a disrupted rhythm. Restore bright days and dark nights.

Many brain networks control sleep. The source names the reticular activating system and the brainstem. Wake-promoting and sleep-promoting systems work against each other. One chemical does not explain sleep.

The source implies that less GABA promotes sleep. That is misleading. GABA is a calming brain chemical. GABA activity actually supports sleep pathways.

sections.heading: What are NREM and REM sleep?
sections.keyIdea: Sleep cycles through three NREM stages and REM, with deep sleep early and longer REM toward morning.
sections.body:
Sleep repeats cycles of NREM and REM during the night. N1 is the drift from waking into sleep. N2 is steady, lighter sleep. N3 is deep, slow-wave sleep. N3 is most common early in the night.

REM periods grow longer later in the night. That is why vivid dreams often happen just before the alarm. During REM the brain is busy, and muscle tone normally drops. Cycles vary from person to person.

The slides use an older system with stages N3 and N4. Today deep sleep is combined into one stage, N3. So there are three NREM stages.

A hospitalized client who is suddenly hard to wake is not just in deep sleep. New low responsiveness needs assessment right away.

rows: Most restorative. Less of it with age.

sections.heading: How does sleep change with age?
sections.keyIdea: Use age norms as context, but judge each client by total sleep and daytime function.
sections.body:
Newborns sleep much of the day in short stretches. Sleep becomes more solid as they grow. Infants vary a lot. Not every baby sleeps through the night by a certain month, so do not compare babies.

Toddlers and preschoolers do best with naps and a steady bedtime routine. School-age children can lose sleep to screens, homework, and caffeine. Teens shift toward later sleep times but still need a lot of sleep.

The course lists about 7–9 hours for adults and 7–8 hours for older adults. Older adults often go to bed and wake earlier. Their sleep is lighter, with more awakenings and less deep sleep. That does not mean they need almost no sleep.

Disabling daytime sleepiness, breathing pauses, or a big new change is not normal aging. It needs evaluation.

rows: Feeding, development, routines, and parent expectations.
Steady rituals, a regular bedtime, and a well-timed nap.
Schedule, screens, caffeine, and school demands.
Shift work, stress, illness, and family duties.
Pain, nocturia, medicines, broken sleep, and daytime function.

sections.heading: How do I assess a sleep problem?
sections.keyIdea: Find out which part of sleep is broken and why before choosing any intervention.
sections.body:
First, sort the problem. Is it trouble falling asleep, waking often, waking too early, or not feeling rested? Ask about usual bedtime, wake time, naps, work, and the bedroom.

Review pain, worry, breathing symptoms, nocturia, medicines, and recent illness. Ask what the client already tried.

Caffeine and nicotine keep people awake. Alcohol may cause sleepiness at first but breaks up sleep later. Never suggest alcohol as a sleep aid.

Compare with the home routine. A night-shift worker awake at 0200 may be on a normal schedule, not “noncompliant.” Snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, and daytime sleepiness need evaluation.
bullets: A sleep diary should record bedtime, wake time, and naps.
It should record awakenings and their causes.
It should record caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, and activity.
It should record symptoms and how the person feels during the day.

sections.heading: What helps clients sleep?
sections.keyIdea: Target the specific cause and cluster nonurgent care, but never skip required monitoring.
sections.body:
Fix what is breaking sleep. Treat pain. Help with position, temperature, and uncomfortable equipment. For nocturia, keep nighttime toileting safe with a clear path and a call light within reach.

Group nonurgent care together when the plan allows. Essential checks, medicines, and tests still happen. Do them quietly, but do not skip them to protect sleep.

Keep familiar bedtime rituals if they are safe, such as prayer or music. For shift workers, teach a dark room, a regular sleep period, and no caffeine or alcohol before sleep.

Evaluate outcomes, not actions. “Room darkened” is an intervention. Fewer awakenings and better alertness are outcomes.
bullets: Keep sleep and wake times regular when possible.
Reduce noise and light at night.
Encourage daylight and activity in the daytime.
Offer relaxation, music, or breathing exercises if the client likes them.
Limit evening screens and caffeine, especially for children and teens.

sections.heading: When is sleepiness a danger sign?
sections.keyIdea: New confusion, hard-to-wake clients, and slowed breathing are emergencies, not sleep problems.
sections.body:
A sleeping pill is not the first answer to every complaint. A client asking for one at 2330 before surgery may be anxious. Ask about the cause first.

Before any sedative, check breathing and recent opioids. Hold the sedative if breathing is already slow or shallow, and report it. Breathing pauses with low oxygen after an opioid outrank other sleep needs.

A client who cannot be awakened is not just in deep sleep. Assess right away for causes such as low blood sugar.

New confusion after a sedative is an adverse effect. Keep the client safe, assess, and report. Do not give more sedation or use restraints as the answer. New confusion in a post-op client also needs a search for a physical cause.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Do not mistake time in bed for sleep, aging for disease, or a dangerous change for tiredness.
sections.body: These look-alike ideas often show up as wrong answers.

rows: Eight hours in bed can include many awakenings.
Earlier, lighter sleep is normal. Breathing pauses and disabling sleepiness are not.
A client who cannot be awakened needs immediate assessment.
Group nonurgent tasks. Keep all required checks.
Treat pain, anxiety, or noise first.
A night-shift worker may have a normal pattern for them.
Alcohol helps onset but breaks up later sleep.
Current staging is N1, N2, N3.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Assess before sedating, and treat any change in alertness or breathing as the priority.
sections.body:
Expect priority items about overnight rounds, sedative safety, and age norms. Select-all items ask about sleep assessment questions or safe interventions.

Sample question: A hospitalized client asks for a sleeping pill after waking many times. The client reports pain at 8/10 and loud hallway noise. What should the nurse do first?
steps: Read the stem: repeated waking, pain 8/10, and hallway noise.
What is it really asking? Should you treat the causes or just sedate?
Key cues: Severe pain and noise are clear, fixable causes.
Wrong options: Requesting sedation and rechecking pain tomorrow leaves severe pain untreated. Starting a diary before fixing the room delays help. Encouraging daytime naps can worsen night sleep.
The answer: Assess the pain, give indicated relief, and reduce the avoidable noise.
Strategy: Look for a cause in the stem and target it before choosing medication.

sections.heading: Worked case: broken sleep and failed teaching
sections.keyIdea: Poor learning after a bad night is a clue to assess sleep, not proof of poor effort.
sections.body:
Mr. T is awake much of the night from pain, frequent toileting, and hallway noise. In the morning he is irritable and cannot focus on new teaching. The chart says “poor participation.” That note does not explain why.

First rule out urgent causes. New confusion or low responsiveness needs assessment, not a sleep hygiene talk.

Then target each cause. Do not assume one sedative will fix several untreated problems. Do not assume all older adults sleep poorly.
steps: Describe his sleep and his alertness now. Is this new?
Find causes: pain, toileting, noise, medicines, and worry.
Treat pain, help with safe toileting, and reduce avoidable noise.
Cluster nonurgent care while keeping required checks.
Reteach when he is alert, and ask him to explain it back in his own words.

check.q: Why is “client stayed in bed all night” not enough evidence that the plan worked?
check.a: It does not show actual sleep, fewer awakenings, restfulness, or daytime function. He may have been awake, in pain, or oversedated.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Use these notes to connect the lesson with your course materials.
bullets: Source: Module 7, Exemplar 7.C, slides 59–68.
Current staging follows the NHLBI sleep phases and stages.
The slides use an older four-stage NREM scheme with N3 and N4. Answer keys use the current three stages.
The slides give approximate timing and percentages. Cycles vary by person.
The source implies less GABA promotes sleep. That is misleading. GABA inhibition supports sleep pathways.

pearls: Hours in bed do not equal hours asleep.
Assess quality, quantity, continuity, and daytime function.
Older adults still need restful sleep.
Cluster nonurgent care while keeping required monitoring.
Check breathing and recent opioids before any sedative.
Bright days and dark nights help reset a disrupted body clock.
redFlags: A client who is newly hard to arouse, acutely confused, or breathing poorly needs prompt assessment.
Breathing pauses with marked daytime sleepiness need follow-up.
Breathing pauses with low oxygen after an opioid are a priority.
New sedation, falls, or confusion after a medicine need reassessment and a report.

checks.q: A client says, “I’m in bed eight hours, but I wake every hour and can’t concentrate.” What does this show?
checks.a: Time in bed is not the same as good sleep. The sleep is broken and is affecting daytime function.

checks.q: How many NREM stages are used today?
checks.a: Three: N1, N2, and N3. The older N3 and N4 stages are now combined as N3.

checks.q: A UAP plans to skip the 0400 vital signs because the client finally fell asleep. What should the nurse say?
checks.a: Required monitoring cannot be skipped. Do it quietly and cluster other nonurgent care.

checks.q: A 79-year-old goes to bed at 2030, wakes at 0430, and feels rested. Is this a problem?
checks.a: Probably not. Earlier sleep timing is common with aging. Judge by total sleep and daytime function.

checks.q: What comes before a request for routine sedation?
checks.a: Assess the sleep pattern and causes, including pain, breathing, anxiety, medicines, substances, and environment.
